title: Cayenne pepper
description: Hot chili pepper used to flavor dishes
wiki_lead:
Cayenne peppers are a group of tapering, 10 to 25 cm long, generally skinny, mostly red-colored pepper varieties, often with a curved tip and somewhat rippled skin, which hang from the bush as opposed to growing upright. Most varieties are generally rated at 30,000 to 50,000 Scoville units.
The fruits are generally dried and ground to make the powdered spice of the same name. However, cayenne powder may be a blend of different types of peppers, quite often not containing cayenne peppers, and may or may not contain the seeds.
Cayenne is used in cooking spicy dishes either as a powder or in its whole form. It is also used as a herbal supplement, due to its active compound, capsaicin. They are also nutritious and they are especially rich in provitamin A, carotenoids and vitamin C.

Cayenne peppers are a group of tapering, 10 to 25 cm long, generally skinny, mostly red-colored pepper varieties, often with a curved tip and somewhat rippled skin, which hang from the bush as opposed to growing upright. Most varieties are generally rated at 30,000 to 50,000 Scoville units.
The fruits are generally dried and ground to make the powdered spice of the same name. However, cayenne powder may be a blend of different types of peppers, quite often not containing cayenne peppers, and may or may not contain the seeds.
Cayenne is used in cooking spicy dishes either as a powder or in its whole form. It is also used as a herbal supplement, due to its active compound, capsaicin. They are also nutritious and they are especially rich in provitamin A, carotenoids and vitamin C.


Etymology
The word cayenne is thought to be a corruption of the word kyynha, meaning "capsicum" in the Old Tupi language once spoken in Brazil. Cayenne, the capital city of French Guiana is related to the name, and may have been named for the pepper or the Cayenne River.
English botanist Nicholas Culpeper used the phrase "cayenne pepper" in 1652.


Taxonomy
The cayenne pepper is a type of Capsicum annuum, as are bell peppers, jalapeños, pimientos, and many others. The genus Capsicum is in the nightshade family, Solanaceae. Cayenne peppers are often said to belong to the frutescens variety, but frutescens peppers are now defined as peppers (such as tabasco peppers) which have fruit which grow upright on the bush. What are known in English as cayenne peppers are therefore, by definition, not frutescens. Culpeper, in his Complete Herbal from 1653, mentions cayenne pepper as a synonym for what he calls "pepper (guinea)". By the end of the 19th century "Guinea pepper" had come to mean bird's eye chili or piri-piri, although he refers to Capsicum peppers in general in his entry.
In the 19th century, modern cayenne peppers were classified as C. longum. This name was later synonymised with C. frutescens. Cayenne powder, however, has generally been made from the bird's eye peppers, in the 19th century classified as C. minimum.


Varieties
Cayenne peppers are long, tapering, 10 to 25 centimetres (4 to 10 in) generally skinny, mostly red-colored peppers, often with a curved tip and somewhat rippled skin, and hang from the bush, as opposed to growing upright.
There are many specific cultivars, such as Cow-horn, Cayenne Sweet, Cayenne Buist's Yellow, Golden Cayenne, Cayenne Carolina, Cayenne Indonesian, Joe's Long, Cayenne Large Red Thick, Cayenne Long Thick Red, Ring of Fire, Cayenne Passion, Cayenne Thomas Jefferson, Cayenne Iberian, Cayenne Turkish, Egyptian Cayenne, Cayenne Violet or NuMex Las Cruces Cayenne. Although most modern cayenne peppers are red, there are yellow and purple varieties and, in the 19th century, yellow varieties were common. grok_lead: Cayenne pepper is a type of moderately hot chili pepper belonging to the species Capsicum annuum in the Solanaceae (nightshade) family, characterized by its long, thin, glossy pods that mature from green to a vibrant red color and measure 2 to 5 inches in length. It originated in South America, with the spice named after the city of Cayenne in French Guiana, where it was historically cultivated, and it registers between 25,000 and 50,000 Scoville Heat Units (SHU), making it significantly hotter than jalapeÃ±os but milder than habaneros. The plant is a frost-tender annual or short-lived perennial herb growing 1 to 3 feet tall, with small white to purple flowers and ovate leaves, producing non-pulpy berry fruits that are typically dried, ground into a fine red powder, or used fresh as a culinary spice. As a staple in global cuisines, cayenne pepper imparts a sharp, fiery heat and is a key ingredient in hot sauces, spice blends like chili powder, and dishes ranging from Indian curries to Mexican salsas and Southern American barbecue. Its powdered form, often simply called cayenne, is versatile for seasoning meats, vegetables, soups, and even chocolates, while fresh pods add color and zest to salads or stir-fries. Beyond culinary applications, cayenne has been valued for its medicinal properties for centuries, particularly due to capsaicin, the active compound responsible for its heat, which may support heart health by lowering blood pressure and reducing inflammation, aid digestion by stimulating gastric juices, and provide pain relief for conditions like arthritis when applied topically. It is also nutrient-dense, offering high levels of vitamins A, C, and B6, along with antioxidants that contribute to its role in traditional remedies for congestion and metabolism support. Cultivation of cayenne pepper thrives in warm climates with full sun and well-drained soil, making it a popular choice for home gardens, containers, or commercial farms in tropical and subtropical regions worldwide. Varieties may differ slightly in pod shape and heat intensity, but the classic cayenne remains prized for its balance of flavor and pungency, influencing both food culture and herbal medicine traditions across continents.
